voice_event.speaker: rzg
voice_event.text: To us Jesus is what the whole church says he is: truly God, truly man, born of the Virgin, crucified under Pontius Pilate, risen on the third day, ascended, and coming again. That was never our own quarrel, not with Rome and not between our own two cities. What is distinctly ours is what we were taught about who is chosen in him. God's own free choice, made before the world began, decides who is saved - not anything foreseen or earned. We hold that as a settled ground, not a threat, and we will not send you searching your own heart for proof of it. Our confession called Christ the mirror in which we see whether we are chosen, and rejected looking for that apart from him. What we actually have of him is not a living chain. No one among us met anyone who met him; fifteen hundred years stand between his own life and ours. What we have is the text, and we hold that it is enough on its own terms.

voice_event.speaker: rzg
voice_event.text: He lived without sin, died bearing the punishment our sin deserved, and rose again on the third day, breaking death's own power. That one sacrifice, offered once, is finished and sufficient - it answers everything. What we refused on both fronts at once was any claim that his sacrifice is repeated at the altar, or that his body is confined to bread. At the Supper, he gives himself truly, by the Spirit's own power, to whoever receives him believing. The bread and cup point to that reality; they do not contain it the way a box contains what is shut inside. Our own founder said it first in 1523: the mass is a remembrance, not a sacrifice. Both our cities spoke together on the same Supper twenty-six years later. We hold both statements as our own. What he did is complete; what we do at the Supper is receive what he has already finished, not repeat it.

voice_event.speaker: rzg
voice_event.text:
Elder. An elder at Geneva was a layperson, not a pastor. An elder held real power on the Consistory, with the pastors. Calvin wrote: “By these governors I mean elders chosen from the people. They join with the pastors to declare censures and to carry out discipline.”

The Consistory itself was our body of pastors and lay elders. It held our whole population's daily conduct to account. We can state the general doctrine plainly. Our own day-to-day case history is not yet something our sources can supply. Who held the final word over church discipline, we never settled between our own two cities. Zurich's council governed church and city together from our first days. Geneva's own Consistory only substantially won its own independence from that kind of claim by 1555. Neither side ever conceded the question to the other.

results.message: Why did your people believe this?

voice_event.speaker: rzg
voice_event.text:
We believed it because Scripture itself says so, and we held Scripture as the one sufficient authority over everything we taught. God's own free choice, made before the world began, decides who is saved - not anything foreseen or earned. Both our cities held this. Geneva built it into a full system. Zurich stated it more briefly, as pastoral comfort. The doctrine was tested aloud and contested. In 1551 a man named Bolsec challenged it publicly at Geneva. That was a real crisis, not a settled question quietly held. The reason we held to it through that challenge is the same reason we held it at all: because the text itself speaks of God's own choosing, and we would not soften what the text says plainly.

We also believed it because it was the ground of a settled life, not a threat. Whoever is joined to Christ by true faith already has, in that faith itself, the only evidence of election anyone is given. Our confession called Christ the mirror in which we see whether we are chosen. A mind turned only on itself finds more of itself, and no bottom to it. We turned it outward instead, toward Christ.

voice_event.speaker: rzg
voice_event.text: We do not keep a saint's life or a martyr's cult, and we will not build you one out of what isn't there. We refused the reverence a saint's life is written to produce. We refused it from our first founding statement onward. What we have instead is the plain record of someone who argued this conviction aloud and died testing it. Our own founder, Huldrych Zwingli, stood before Zurich's council and six hundred priests and laymen in 1523. He defended his case from Scripture until the council itself ruled for it and told every priest in its land to preach the same way. Eight years later he rode out to battle on 11 October 1531 and was killed that afternoon. His friend Myconius wrote down what he remembered. That is as close as we come to remembering anyone: a plain, contemporary account. An argument won before a city council, or a pastor killed in the war that tested our own convictions. Never a story shaped to be venerated.

voice_event.speaker: rzg
voice_event.text:
We answered what Scripture alone may bind a church to believe, and we answered it two ways. At Zurich, that conviction was argued aloud before the council and six hundred priests and laymen, until the council itself said what the text had yielded. At Geneva, it was built up article by article and taught to everyone through the Catechism. We do not read these as two churches that happen to agree. We read them as one authority, enacted twice by two cities that did not need to share a method. What we will not tell you is that the two methods ever became one arrangement. Zurich's council governed church and city together. Geneva's Consistory fought for its independence from that kind of council control, and only by 1555 substantially won it. We hold that unresolved, in the same breath as the conviction itself, because it is also true.

What we cannot walk you through is an ordinary day among us. What survives from our hand is confession, catechism, disputation record, and confessional argument. How a Sunday service felt to sit through, what a Consistory summons felt like to receive: none of that has reached us.
